question: In a set of doubles or triples, which trailer is most likely to turn over due to the crack-the-whip effect?
choice_a: The last trailer in the combination
explanation: The manual states that doubles and triples are more likely to turn over than other combination vehicles because of the crack-the-whip effect, and the last trailer in a combination is most likely to turn over.
source_note: Arizona Commercial Driver License Manual (AAMVA 2005/2022 CDL Testing System, ADOT MVD, Revised 01/2026), Section 7 - Doubles and Triples, p. 7-1

question: Why does the manual warn that a safe curve speed for a straight truck or single-trailer combination may be too fast for a set of doubles or triples?
choice_a: Doubles and triples are legally restricted to slower posted speeds everywhere
choice_b: Doubles and triples always have better traction than single trailers
choice_c: There is no real difference; the warning only applies to tank vehicles
choice_d: Doubles and triples are less stable than other commercial vehicles and can roll over more easily
explanation: The manual explains that doubles/triples are less stable than other commercial vehicles, so drivers must steer gently and go slowly around corners, ramps, and curves, at speeds that may be slower than what would be safe for a single trailer.
source_note: Arizona Commercial Driver License Manual (AAMVA 2005/2022 CDL Testing System, ADOT MVD, Revised 01/2026), Section 7 - Doubles and Triples, p. 7-1

question: Why does the manual emphasize inspecting doubles and triples especially thoroughly?
choice_a: There are more critical parts to check when you have two or three trailers
choice_b: Inspections are only required for tank-type doubles
choice_c: Doubles and triples do not require a pre-trip inspection under federal rules
choice_d: Only the rearmost trailer needs to be inspected
explanation: The manual states there are more critical parts to check when pulling two or three trailers, and instructs drivers to check them all following the described procedures.
source_note: Arizona Commercial Driver License Manual (AAMVA 2005/2022 CDL Testing System, ADOT MVD, Revised 01/2026), Section 7 - Doubles and Triples, p. 7-1

question: Why do doubles and triples require more following distance and larger gaps than other commercial vehicles?
choice_a: Their brakes react faster than a single trailer's brakes
choice_b: They take up more space, are longer, and cannot be turned or stopped as suddenly as other vehicles
choice_c: They are exempt from following distance rules under CDL regulations
choice_d: They have shorter stopping distances than single vehicles
explanation: The manual says doubles and triples take up more space than other commercial vehicles because they are longer and can't be turned or stopped suddenly, so drivers should allow more following distance and larger gaps before entering or crossing traffic.
source_note: Arizona Commercial Driver License Manual (AAMVA 2005/2022 CDL Testing System, ADOT MVD, Revised 01/2026), Section 7 - Doubles and Triples, p. 7-1

question: What makes doubles and triples especially challenging to drive in bad weather, slippery conditions, and mountain driving?
choice_a: They are exempt from tire chain requirements
choice_b: Greater length and more dead axles to pull with the drive axles, which increases the chance of skids and loss of traction
choice_c: They automatically shift into a low gear that reduces control
choice_d: Their trailers have no brakes at all
explanation: The manual explains that with doubles and triples you have greater length and more dead axles to pull with your drive axles than other drivers, creating more chance for skids and loss of traction in adverse conditions.
source_note: Arizona Commercial Driver License Manual (AAMVA 2005/2022 CDL Testing System, ADOT MVD, Revised 01/2026), Section 7 - Doubles and Triples, p. 7-1

question: What parking advice does the manual give specifically for doubles and triples?
choice_a: Always back into the parking spot to save time
choice_b: Park only at designated tank-vehicle facilities
choice_c: Use the trailer hand valve to lock all trailer wheels whenever parked
choice_d: Avoid getting into a spot you cannot pull straight through, and be aware of how the parking lot is arranged
explanation: The manual warns drivers to make sure they do not get into a spot they cannot pull straight through, and to be aware of how parking lots are arranged in order to avoid a long and difficult escape.
source_note: Arizona Commercial Driver License Manual (AAMVA 2005/2022 CDL Testing System, ADOT MVD, Revised 01/2026), Section 7 - Doubles and Triples, p. 7-1

topic: Antilock Brake Systems on Converter Dollies
question: Converter dollies built on or after what date are required to have antilock brakes, and how is this indicated?
choice_a: January 1, 2000; by a red lamp on the right side of the dolly
choice_b: Converter dollies are never required to have ABS
choice_c: 1975; by a green lamp on the dolly's tongue
choice_d: March 1, 1998; by a yellow lamp on the left side of the dolly
explanation: The manual states that converter dollies built on or after March 1, 1998, are required to have antilock brakes, and these dollies will have a yellow lamp on the left side of the dolly.
source_note: Arizona Commercial Driver License Manual (AAMVA 2005/2022 CDL Testing System, ADOT MVD, Revised 01/2026), Section 7 - Doubles and Triples, p. 7-1

question: How does the manual define a converter dolly?
choice_a: A backup electrical generator for trailer running lights
choice_b: A type of spring-loaded parking brake control
choice_c: A coupling device of one or two axles and a fifth wheel used to couple a semitrailer to the rear of a tractor-trailer combination, forming a double bottom rig
choice_d: A hydraulic lift used only on tank vehicles to raise the load
explanation: The manual defines a converter dolly as a coupling device of one or two axles and a fifth wheel by which a semitrailer can be coupled to the rear of a tractor-trailer combination, forming a double bottom rig.
source_note: Arizona Commercial Driver License Manual (AAMVA 2005/2022 CDL Testing System, ADOT MVD, Revised 01/2026), Section 7 - Doubles and Triples, p. 7-1

question: For the safest handling on the road when pulling doubles, where should the more heavily loaded semitrailer be positioned?
choice_a: In the rear position, behind the lighter trailer
choice_b: Position makes no difference to handling
choice_c: In the first position, directly behind the tractor
choice_d: Weight should always be split evenly between the two trailers
explanation: The manual states that for the safest handling on the road, the more heavily loaded semitrailer should be in the first position behind the tractor, with the lighter trailer in the rear.
source_note: Arizona Commercial Driver License Manual (AAMVA 2005/2022 CDL Testing System, ADOT MVD, Revised 01/2026), Section 7 - Doubles and Triples, p. 7-1

question: If the second (rear) trailer in a set of doubles does not have spring brakes, how does the manual say a driver can set its emergency brakes before coupling the converter dolly?
choice_a: There is no way to secure a trailer that lacks spring brakes
choice_b: Only wheel chocks may ever be used, with no other method available
choice_c: Drive the tractor close to the trailer, connect the emergency line to charge the trailer air tank, then disconnect the emergency line
choice_d: Continuously hold the trailer hand valve in the applied position
explanation: The manual explains that if the second trailer lacks spring brakes, you can drive the tractor close to it, connect the emergency line, charge the trailer air tank, and disconnect the emergency line, which sets the trailer emergency brakes if the slack adjusters are correctly set; chock the wheels if there is any doubt.
source_note: Arizona Commercial Driver License Manual (AAMVA 2005/2022 CDL Testing System, ADOT MVD, Revised 01/2026), Section 7 - Doubles and Triples, p. 7-1

question: When positioning a converter dolly to couple it to the rear trailer, what must be true about the trailer's height?
choice_a: The trailer must be resting fully on the ground with zero clearance from the dolly
choice_b: Trailer height has no bearing on dolly coupling
choice_c: It must be significantly higher than the dolly's fifth wheel
choice_d: It must be slightly lower than the center of the dolly's fifth wheel, so the trailer is raised slightly when the dolly is pushed under it
explanation: The manual states the trailer height must be slightly lower than the center of the fifth wheel, so the trailer is raised slightly when the dolly is pushed under it.
source_note: Arizona Commercial Driver License Manual (AAMVA 2005/2022 CDL Testing System, ADOT MVD, Revised 01/2026), Section 7 - Doubles and Triples, p. 7-2

question: Why does the manual warn drivers to never unlock the pintle hook while the converter dolly is still under the rear trailer?
choice_a: The dolly tow bar may fly up, possibly causing injury and making it very difficult to re-couple
choice_b: It will drain the trailer's air tanks instantly
choice_c: It will automatically trigger the tractor protection valve
choice_d: It has no real risk and is just a recommended habit
explanation: The manual specifically warns to never unlock the pintle hook with the dolly still under the rear trailer, because the dolly tow bar may fly up, possibly causing injury and making it very difficult to re-couple.
source_note: Arizona Commercial Driver License Manual (AAMVA 2005/2022 CDL Testing System, ADOT MVD, Revised 01/2026), Section 7 - Doubles and Triples, p. 7-3

question: On a set of doubles or triples, how should the shut-off valves at the rear of the trailers, in the service and emergency lines, be set?
choice_a: All shut-off valves on every trailer should always be closed
choice_b: All shut-off valves on every trailer should always be open, including the last trailer
choice_c: Only the dolly's valves matter; the trailer valves can be left in any position
choice_d: Rear of the front trailer(s) should be OPEN; rear of the last trailer should be CLOSED
explanation: The manual's inspection checklist for doubles and triples states that shut-off valves at the rear of front trailers should be OPEN, while the rear of the last trailer should be CLOSED.
source_note: Arizona Commercial Driver License Manual (AAMVA 2005/2022 CDL Testing System, ADOT MVD, Revised 01/2026), Section 7 - Doubles and Triples, p. 7-3

question: During a pre-trip inspection of a converter dolly, what position should the dolly's air tank drain valve be in?
choice_d: Converter dollies do not have a drain valve
explanation: The manual's inspection checklist specifies that the converter dolly air tank drain valve should be CLOSED.
source_note: Arizona Commercial Driver License Manual (AAMVA 2005/2022 CDL Testing System, ADOT MVD, Revised 01/2026), Section 7 - Doubles and Triples, p. 7-3

question: When checking that air flows all the way to the back of a set of doubles or triples, what should the driver do at the emergency line shut-off valve at the rear of the last trailer?
choice_a: Open it and listen for escaping air, which shows the entire system is charged
choice_b: Immediately drive at highway speed to test the brakes under load
choice_c: Leave it closed at all times and never test it
choice_d: Disconnect the electrical cord instead of testing the air valve
explanation: The manual explains that after pushing in the red trailer air supply knob, you should go to the rear of the rig, open the emergency line shut-off valve at the rear of the last trailer, and listen for air escaping to confirm the entire system is charged.
source_note: Arizona Commercial Driver License Manual (AAMVA 2005/2022 CDL Testing System, ADOT MVD, Revised 01/2026), Section 7 - Doubles and Triples, p. 7-4
